newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa industrials seen up next week, golds dull.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa industrials seen up next week, golds dull.

text.p: South African gold shares will remain enslaved by a dull bullion price next week, but industrial stocks should ride a wave of strong world markets and dominate trade on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

Portfolio managers and dealers said on Friday that futures, currently trading a a premium to cash, could also help pump up industrials next week while a steady rand -- if maintained -- could tempt back more foreigners.

"World markets are extremely strong right now. I don't think that should change overnight. They're strong and I think the buying (in industrials) will carry on," said Raymond Goss, portfolio manager at Irish & Co Ltd.
"We are going through a slightly better time now, a lot of stocks will carry on running. I do expect volumes to carry on increasing and for our market to be stronger."
But some dealers said that Wall Street's alternate stronger and softer finishes this last weeek had unnerved some investors who were now waiting for clearer signs of direction.
Bullion, as an investment, looked likely to be ignored for a while longer as, with little world inflation, gold was unwanted as a hedge against inflation.
Consequently, gold shares would see little trade next week, hopping or dipping to the metal price's whims.

"It's quite obvious that foreigners are keener on our industrial shares than our mining shares. The general consensus is that the rand is likely to stabilise and this could also take the shine off mining shares," said Denzil Newman of Syfrets Managed Assets.
Gold producers, who benefited when the rand lost 29 percent against the dollar in 1996, are set for a tougher 1997 if the rand steadies and dollar gold prices remain weak.

Commentators said that a number of negative factors could cloud the South African market, including the government's foreign policy and the worrying implications of a growing money market shortage, now back over 10 billion rand.

This week's dispute between President Nelson Mandela and the U.S. over South Africa's plan to sell arms to Syria could still impact on the rand, which, if it weakened, could take its pound of flesh off industrial shares.
"If the rand dips back towards the 4.70 mark (on the dollar), which is a possibility especially with the Syrian arms deal, we may see equities come under some pressure," Goss said.
Industrial shares would be open to the influence of futures-related activity next week.
Dealers said that futures players were likely to buy shares next week as contracts were starting to trade at an increasing premium to underlying stocks.
"There is a lot of futures related activity, mainly on the all-share and industrial indices," said Dominick Rey, a senior dealer at Investec Fergusson Bros.

"(Futures contracts) are currently trading just above fair value and the moment that gap widens, whereby the futures are trading at a premium of plus 50 points to fair value, we are going to see them coming to buy shares aggressively," he added.
But Rey added that South African stocks were exceptionally volatile and that any rise could rapidly be reveresed.

"The industrials are looking nice and firm, but like anything, this can reverse to a reverse arbitrage situation overnight where you've suddenly got a discount to fair value and the futures guys start punishing the shares.
"That's the problem with our market. It's exceptionally volatile with the futures-related play and it's irrelevant what the fundamentals are saying," Rey said.
